Dragon Tiger Explained: The Simplest Card Game on the Casino Floor and Its House Edge

Published November 7, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Most casino card games build in rounds of decisions — hit or stand, raise or fold, draw a third card or stand pat. Dragon Tiger strips all of that away. One card goes to "Dragon," one card goes to "Tiger," whichever is higher wins, and the whole hand is over in seconds. That simplicity is exactly why it's become a live-dealer staple, and it's also why the betting menu around that one comparison hides some of the widest house-edge gaps of any game on the floor.

How a hand of Dragon Tiger actually works

Dealt from a standard shoe of six to eight decks, Dragon Tiger ranks cards Ace (low) through King (high) with suits ignored entirely — a 9 of hearts and a 9 of spades are identical for scoring purposes. The dealer burns a card, then deals exactly one card face-up to the position marked Dragon and one to the position marked Tiger. Higher rank wins; that's the entire game. There's no drawing, no player decision once bets are placed, and no hidden information — both cards are visible before the round resolves, which is part of why it plays so fast at a live table.

The tie rule that quietly sets the house edge

The one rule that does all the heavy lifting in Dragon Tiger's math is what happens when Dragon and Tiger are dealt the same rank. Under the standard rule used at most live-dealer tables, a tie doesn't push the Dragon and Tiger bets the way a tied hand pushes in blackjack — instead, those two bets each lose half their stake. A $20 Dragon bet that ties loses $10 and keeps $10. That half-loss, applied across the roughly 1-in-13 hands that tie, is the entire source of the house's edge on the main bet — remove it and Dragon vs. Tiger would be a near-perfect coin flip.

Worth knowing: because ties only cost half a bet instead of the whole thing, Dragon Tiger's main bet ends up with one of the lowest house edges of any even-money proposition in the casino — lower than a standard roulette even-money bet and in the same neighborhood as baccarat.

Dragon and Tiger bets: the math behind 3.73%

With ties occurring on roughly 1 of every 13 hands (both positions landing on the same rank), and each tie costing a Dragon or Tiger bettor half their stake instead of the full amount, the long-run house edge on either side works out to approximately 3.73%. That number holds whether you bet Dragon or Tiger — the two sides are symmetric, so there's no "better" side to back based on the game's structure alone.

The Tie bet: a much bigger number than it looks

The Tie bet looks tempting because of the payout — 8:1 is a common number at live-dealer tables — but that payout is nowhere near generous enough given how rarely a true tie actually lands. At roughly a 1-in-13 chance, fair odds on a tie bet would need to pay closer to 12:1 just to break even before the house takes its cut. Paying only 8:1 against those real odds is what pushes the Tie bet's house edge up into the low 30s percent, making it one of the worst single wagers on an otherwise fairly player-friendly game. A handful of tables offer 11:1 on the Tie, which narrows the edge but still leaves it well above the main Dragon/Tiger bet.

Big/Small and suited side bets

Many Dragon Tiger tables also spread a Big/Small bet, wagering on whether the next card dealt (to either position, depending on the table's rule) lands 8 through King (Big) or Ace through 6 (Small), with 7 as a losing number for both sides. Because 7 removes a slice of outcomes from both bets rather than favoring one side, Big and Small each carry a modest house edge in roughly the same range as the main Dragon/Tiger wager. A Suited Tie bet — requiring the tied cards to also share a suit — pays far more than a plain tie, commonly around 50:1, but the added condition makes it rarer still, and the exact edge varies more by casino than any other bet on the table. Always check a specific table's posted payout table before assuming a "standard" number applies.

A worked example across 1,000 hands

Picture flat-betting $10 on Dragon across 1,000 hands. Ignoring ties, Dragon wins roughly 462 hands and loses roughly 462 (the remaining ~76 are ties), for a rough breakeven on the non-tie hands. On the 76 tie hands, the Dragon bet loses half its stake — $5 each — for a total of about $380 lost purely to the tie rule, against $10,000 wagered. That lines up closely with the ~3.73% theoretical edge once you divide $380 by $10,000. Compare that to flat-betting the same $10 on Tie for 1,000 hands: roughly 76 wins at 8:1 profit ($80 each, or about $6,080 total) against 924 losses of $10 each ($9,240), netting a loss of roughly $3,160 — a dramatically worse outcome for the same total action, which is the gap between a 3.73% edge and a ~32% one made concrete.

Common mistakes new players make

The most common mistake is treating the Tie payout as a "bonus" worth chasing because it feels like a side opportunity rather than recognizing it as the single worst bet on the table mathematically. The second is assuming Dragon and Tiger aren't truly symmetric and looking for a pattern (a "hot" side) in recent results — the cards are reshuffled or drawn fresh each round, and nothing about a prior hand changes the next one's odds. Treat Dragon Tiger as what it is: a fast, low-edge coin-flip game on the main bet, with side bets that exist almost entirely to fund the low edge on that main wager.

A 3.73% edge is still a house edge — over enough hands, the math favors the casino on every bet at this table. Play Dragon Tiger as fast-paced entertainment with a budget set in advance, and see our responsible gambling resources for tools to manage your limits.

Frequently asked questions

Is Dragon Tiger just a simplified version of baccarat?

They share a visual style and a similar tie rule, but Dragon Tiger deals only one card per side with no drawing rules at all, while baccarat deals two or three cards per hand and totals them. Dragon Tiger is considerably simpler and faster.

Does it matter whether I bet Dragon or Tiger?

No. Both positions are dealt from the same shoe under identical rules, so the house edge is mathematically identical on either side — any preference is purely personal, not strategic.

Why do some tables pay 11:1 on Tie instead of 8:1?

It's a competitive variation some operators use to make the Tie bet less punishing and more attractive to players. It still carries a high house edge relative to the main bet, just a somewhat smaller one than the 8:1 version.

Can card counting work on Dragon Tiger the way it can on blackjack?

Not meaningfully. With six to eight decks in play and only rank (not full card composition) mattering for the outcome, there isn't a practical edge to be gained by tracking the shoe the way there can be in single or double-deck blackjack.
